analysis.one_liner: Gives patients control over their own medical records, with civil and criminal penalties for misuse.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 1996 with 23 cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, and died without ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first comprehensive federal privacy law for medical records. Patients could inspect and correct their own records, and doctors, insurers, employers, and others could not share identifiable health information without a specific, signed, revocable consent. It set security rules for computerized records, barred companies from requiring patients to sign away privacy as a condition of care or employment, and attached fines, lawsuits, and prison terms to violations. The bill never advanced past its first committee referrals and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients. Anyone who sees a doctor, fills a prescription, or holds insurance would gain the right to see and correct their own records, know who their information was shared with, and sue or see criminal charges brought against people who misuse it. The bill also restricted employer and insurer access to health records, limited law enforcement access to a high evidentiary bar, and specifically addressed genetic information, which can reveal facts about relatives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with medical and genetic records

how_it_helps.text: Patients would gain the right to inspect and copy their own health information within 30 days, and to correct or amend errors within 45 days, with the right to attach a statement of disagreement if the record holder refuses.

Disclosures would be allowed only with a written authorization naming what is shared, with whom, and why — or in a short list of exceptions such as emergencies, public health, and oversight — and every disclosure would be limited to the minimum information necessary.

Providers, insurers, and employers could not condition treatment, payment, or a job on a patient signing a broad disclosure authorization, and could not retaliate against anyone exercising these rights.

Record holders would have to build administrative, technical, and physical safeguards for computerized records, keep audit trails of access attempts, and could not use Social Security numbers to identify health records.

Violations would carry civil penalties up to $150,000 per year, and up to $500,000 plus exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid when violations are a general business practice; individuals could sue for $25,000–$50,000 in liquidated damages plus punitive damages; knowingly selling or misusing records for gain could bring up to 10 years in prison.

The bill's findings noted there was little federal protection for health information, that state protection varied widely, and that computerized records and genetic testing created new risks of unauthorized access and misuse.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, health plans, employers, schools, and other 'health information trustees' would bear the cost of building safeguards, tracking disclosures, and processing patient requests, and would lose their largely unrestricted ability to use and share identifiable health data. Health care providers and researchers would absorb compliance paperwork, and law enforcement would face a much higher bar — clear and convincing evidence plus court procedures — to obtain records.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would fall heavily on doctor's offices, hospitals, and insurers: written notices of information practices, separate consent forms for treatment and payment, seven-year record retention, audit trails, and 30- and 45-day response deadlines for patient requests.

Law enforcement would face strict limits: agents could not obtain identifiable health records without meeting a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard, would face court challenge procedures with possible fee awards against them, and could not use records for investigations unrelated to the original purpose.

Researchers would generally need institutional review board approval and, for identifiable records, patient authorization, which could slow some studies — though the bill allowed coded and nonidentifiable data to be used with IRB approval alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are broad and durable — the bill would have set a national floor covering everyone's medical and genetic records at a time when federal protection was nearly nonexistent. The costs are real but ordinary regulatory costs: compliance paperwork, some friction for research and law enforcement. The bill was carefully drawn to blunt the strongest objections — it preserved stronger state privacy laws rather than overriding them, allowed emergency and public-health disclosures, and let coded data flow to researchers without individual consent. On balance it is a well-designed consumer protection bill whose main cost falls on the industries that were profiting from unrestricted use of patient data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to subcommittees, and it sat there until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott, a physician, introduced the bill on May 16, 1996, joined by Reps. Serrano and Pelosi as original sponsors.
The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Government Reform and Oversight Committee on the day of introduction.
Within a week, each committee referred it onward — to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology on May 22 and the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on May 24.
No further action of any kind appears in the record; the bill died at the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997, having never reached a committee vote or the House floor.

The bill's own findings acknowledged that federal protection of health information confidentiality was minimal and state protection varied greatly — a gap that remained unfilled by this bill's failure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers, and companies that compile and trade health information continued operating with no comprehensive federal privacy rules, while patients went on without the rights this bill would have granted them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, employers, and health data companies

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and 21 of the 23 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; only 2 of 236 House Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to use and share identifiable patient records without specific written consent, and pattern violators could be barred from Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs. Their unrestricted access to claims and underwriting data — a valuable business asset — would have been cut back.

Employers holding employee health information would be covered as 'health information trustees' and could not condition employment on signing a disclosure authorization. This would close a channel through which employers could learn workers' medical and genetic details.

industries.industry: Insurance support organizations and medical data bureaus
industries.note: Companies that assemble and sell health information to insurers are explicitly named and regulated by the bill, with authorization requirements, audit duties, and penalties. Their core business of compiling patient data would have faced federal limits for the first time.

Providers would bear the heaviest compliance load — notices, separate consent forms, safeguards, and response deadlines — but would also get liability protection for good-faith disclosures and clearer rules for court and law-enforcement access to records.

Research access to identifiable records would require review board approval and, in most cases, patient authorization, adding friction; but coded and nonidentifiable data could flow with board approval alone, and the bill set clear rules where none existed.

Police and prosecutors would need clear and convincing evidence that records are necessary, and individuals would get notice and a right to challenge warrants, with fees available against the government if they prevail. This raises the cost of obtaining medical records for investigations.
